Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Aerospace & Defense Inc., or GA&D, Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, the instructions are to press star one on your telephone keypad if you would like to join the queue. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Lisa Chen, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to GA&D's Q3 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are David Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Steve Harlan, Chief Financial Officer; Maria Gonzalez, Chief Operating Officer; and Dr. Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those discussed today.

David Reynolds:
Thank you, Lisa, and good morning, everyone. GA&D delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, space, and commercial aviation. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, I'll highlight progress in key areas: program margins and cost performance analysis, revenue and earnings guidance by segment, free cash flow generation and utilization, aftermarket and services revenue growth, and the performance of our priority defense programs.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next Generation Air Dominance, or NGAD, program and its potential to accelerate our future growth trajectory. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, including hypersonics and integrated air defense, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily amid rising global flight hours. With that, I'll turn it over to Steve for a deeper dive into our financial results.

Steve Harlan:
Thank you, David, and good morning, everyone. Let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $6.9 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Our diluted earnings per share were $2.50. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $15 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at the high end, reflecting our confidence in execution. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives like digital engineering and supply chain resilience. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through our quarterly dividend and share repurchases, having deployed over $2.2 billion year-to-date.

Our specific financial highlights include a gross margin of 22.5%, operating income of $823 million, and free cash flow of $1.4 billion.

To provide more context, let me start with program margins and cost performance analysis, which remain a cornerstone of our profitability amid a dynamic macroeconomic and geopolitical landscape. Our overall segment-adjusted operating margins expanded by 120 basis points year-over-year to 11.8% in Q3, driven by maturing fixed-price contracts, disciplined estimate-at-completion, or EAC, management, and proactive cost-reduction efforts across our portfolio.

In our Defense Systems segment, which accounted for 62% of Q3 revenue at $4.2 billion, margins reached a robust 12.4%, up 150 basis points from last year. This reflects production learning curves on cornerstone programs. For example, our F-47 Joint Strike Partner program—a next-generation fifth-generation fighter collaborative effort similar to the NGAD architecture we're pursuing with the U.S. Air Force—saw low-rate initial production Lot 5 achieve a 10.2% program margin, ahead of our 9.5% EAC, due to a 15% reduction in touch labor hours per airframe through automated composite layup and digital twin simulations. We've banked over $180 million in performance fees year-to-date on this cost-plus-incentive-fee contract, with cumulative cost variance now at a favorable +2.8% against baseline.

On missiles and precision weapons, our hypersonic glide vehicle program—scaled for peer adversaries like advanced Patriot MSE equivalents—expanded margins to 13.1%, supported by $250 million in material cost savings from dual-sourcing rare earths at our reshored Kentucky facility. We did incur a $45 million other indirect research adjustment on the legacy THAAD Block II interceptor from titanium supply chain inflation, resulting in an 8.7% margin there. Overall, Defense cost performance is trending positively: our segment-wide Cost Performance Index stands at 1.05, with 85% of our $28 billion backlog now under firm fixed-price terms that will mature into higher-margin sustainment phases.

Moving to Space & Launch Systems, 18% of revenue at $1.3 billion, margins held steady at 10.2% despite propulsion qualification delays. Our Vulcan Centaur heavy-lift equivalent delivered an 11.5% margin on five Q3 missions, where RD-180 successor engines benefited from additive-manufactured nozzles that cut material costs by 22%. Cost growth on the crewed lunar lander variant—mirroring NASA's Artemis Human Landing System—was contained to 3% over EAC using agile SCRUM methodologies in our software-defined avionics stack. This segment is particularly strong in EMEA, where UK Space Command contracts added $120 million in high-margin smallsat dispensers, offsetting U.S. government sequestration risks.

Commercial Aviation, 20% of revenue at $1.4 billion, posted 9.6% margins—a 200 basis point improvement despite OEM supply chain issues. Our CFM RISE open-rotor demonstrator equivalent hit 8.9% margins, with ultrahigh-bypass fan efficiency gains from AI-optimized blade aerodynamics reducing certification life-cycle costs by 18%. Boeing 777X and Airbus A350 ramps remain challenging, but our nacelle and winglet aftermarket MRO business grew 25% year-over-year, delivering 14.2% margins on performance-based logistics contracts. This is bolstered by our AeroLean 2.0 initiative—deploying Industry 4.0 cobots across three U.S. and one India facility—yielding $320 million in annual run-rate savings, mainly in non-recurring engineering.

Regionally, U.S. DoD topline growth from the FY24 National Defense Authorization Act's $886 billion budget supported 60% of our Defense wins, while NATO's 2% GDP pledge drove €450 million in European missile co-production deals akin to those with Rheinmetall and MBDA. In Asia-Pacific, South China Sea tensions accelerated $200 million in F-47 export lots to Indo-Pacific allies, with 11% margins thanks to offset manufacturing in Australia. Inflation is a watch item—our passthrough clauses captured 85% of the 4.2% blended CPI increase—but skilled welder shortages drove wage escalation to 6.5%, offset by our apprenticeship pipeline training 2,500 new hires on hypersonic fabrication tech.

Strategically, we're focused on margin accretion through backlog quality, where 92% of our $92 billion backlog is fixed-price or incentive-fee with average margin potential of 12.5% versus 10.8% last year; supply chain resilience, derisking 70% of criticals via nearshoring including a new Polish titanium mill JV cutting lead times 40%; and tech infusion, with $450 million in our Enterprise Digital Backbone accelerating EAC convergence by 25% and positioning us for Joint All-Domain Command and Control primes.

Looking forward, we guide Q4 segment margins to 12.0-12.3%, full-year at 11.5% implying 250 basis points expansion. Risks include potential U.S. Continuing Resolutions delaying lot awards and commercial engine certification slips, but our $15 billion cash and 2.1x net debt-to-EBITDA provide dry powder for bolt-on M&A in C4ISR. We're on track for 15%+ return on invested capital on new wins by 2026.

Building on that, let's discuss revenue and earnings guidance by segment. For Defense Systems, we expect full-year revenue of $11.2 to $11.5 billion with operating margins of 13.5-14.0%, driven by priority programs and sustainment growth. Space & Launch Systems guidance is $5.0 to $5.3 billion at 10.5-11.0% margins, factoring in mission cadence and EMEA wins. Commercial Aviation is guided to $5.8 to $6.0 billion with margins expanding to 10.0-10.5%, supported by aftermarket ramp and AeroLean efficiencies. Overall company revenue guidance is $28.5 to $29.0 billion, with adjusted operating margins of 11.8-12.0% and EPS of $10.20 to $10.40. These reflect our $92 billion backlog, book-to-bill of 1.2x, and favorable fixed-price mix.

Shifting to the performance of our priority defense programs, which drove $2.8 billion in Q3 revenue—up 15% year-over-year and 8% sequentially, or 62% of total segment revenue. Adjusted operating margins expanded 120 basis points to 14.2%, from higher-volume Lot 18 production on fixed-wing platforms, sustainment mix shifts, and cost discipline amid supply pressures.

Our NGAD family, including F-35 Block 4 modernization and collaborative combat aircraft demonstrators, generated $1.1 billion, up 22% year-over-year, on DoD authority to proceed with digital engineering prototypes and ramps to 156 aircraft annually across partners. First-article test acceptance hit 95% of Block 4 hardware ahead of schedule, with TR-3 combat testing underway at Edwards AFB. Margins reached 15.8%, up from 13.9%, mitigating titanium delays via dual-sourcing with suppliers like Precision Castparts. NGAD's open mission systems integrate AI-driven loyal wingman drones like XQ-58 Valkyrie derivatives, targeting the $100 billion Penetrating Counter-Air market through 2040. Exports to UK and Japan under the Global Combat Air Programme add $4.2 billion funded backlog.

Hypersonics and precision strike, including AGM-183A ARRW and HAWC derivatives, posted $650 million, up 28% year-over-year, following successful B-52 and F-15 flight tests from Eglin. Lot 2 full-rate production is authorized, with glide-body yields over 98% via additive manufacturing in Camden, Arkansas. The $12.5 billion backlog includes Indo-Pacific demand from AUKUS Pillar 2 and Japan's JASSM-ER. Margins at 16.5% despite rare earth inflation, hedged 85% through 2025. We're investing $250 million in FY24 R&D for hypersonic wind tunnels targeting Mach 12+ velocities against DF-17 equivalents.

Integrated air and missile defense, led by Next-Gen Interceptor and PAC-3 MSE, delivered $550 million, up 12%. NGI ground tests succeeded in four of five exo-atmospheric trials, unlocking $2.8 billion FY24 funding. PAC-3 hit 180 quarterly missiles for Ukraine and NATO's Eastern Flank—Poland added $1.2 billion. Middle East co-productions with Israel and Saudi Arabia, plus Europe's $50 billion spend, favor our LTAMDS radars. Margins expanded to 13.9% with 40% sustainment mix.

Undersea warfare—Virginia-class Block V and Columbia-class—contributed $500 million, flat year-over-year but up sequentially from Groton welding efficiencies. SSN-796 Hyman G. Rickover delivered on time via 1,200 apprentices. Columbia's first pressure hull is 20% ahead of 2027 milestones, with $18 billion funded backlog. Public-private partnerships target 2.0 subs/year by 2028; AUKUS adds $3.5 billion options.

Total defense backlog is $52.4 billion, up 9%, 45% funded, book-to-bill 1.3x. Supply inflation up 3% quarter-over-quarter on electronics is buffered by $1.2 billion inventory and hedging. Digital twins cut test costs 25%. We guide FY24 defense revenue to $11.2-$11.5 billion, margins 13.5-14.0%, with NGAD and hypersonics at 18-20% CAGR.

Another standout is aftermarket and services revenue growth, up 17% year-over-year to $2.8 billion—the sixth straight double-digit quarter. This high-margin business now 42% of total revenue, up from 38%.

Commercial aviation aftermarket surged 22% to $1.6 billion on global flight hours at 95% pre-pandemic per IATA. Narrowbodies like 737 and A320 drive CFM LEAP engine shop visits up 15% with 12+ hour utilizations. Heavy maintenance and performance restoration benefited from 8% better time-on-wing via blade refurb tech.

Our GAD Digital Twin platform covers 70% of the engine base, partnering with GE and Safran for AI predictive analytics slashing unplanned removals 25% and boosting dispatch to 99.7%. Airlines like Southwest and Delta extend LTSAs at 28%+ margins. Boeing 737 MAX return added $150 million from winglets and thrust reversers.

Defense services grew 12% to $1.2 billion on $45 billion sustainment backlog. F-35 PBL with Lockheed and JPO hit $650 million, up 14%, as fleet hours top 500,000 yearly. Autonomous monitoring on ALIS/ODIN cut failures 18%, enabling depot upsells. Black Hawk UH-60M overhauls for U.S. Army and Poland added $200 million at 95% capacity.

North America at 55% grew 19% on MRO demand; Europe 16% via Ryanair, Lufthansa, Frankfurt facility; APAC 25% to $550 million from IndiGo 737 MAX and ANA LEAPs; emerging markets up 30% on 777X/A350 with PMAs.

Our Services First pivot invested $500 million in Singapore and San Antonio MRO, totaling 1.2 million man-hours. Lead times eased to 38 weeks. Margins hit 26.5%, up 210 bps, from digital services (35%) and composites integration. FCF conversion over 95%, funding $400 million repurchases.

We see 15-18% FY24 growth on $50 billion backlog, 3.5x coverage. Tailwinds: aging fleets (12-year average), MRO premiums, $170 billion NDAA sustainment. Diversification—no client over 10%—mitigates risks.

Finally, on free cash flow generation and utilization—FCF as cash from operations minus CapEx. Q3 FCF was $1.4 billion, up 75% from $800 million last year, beating forecast by $200 million; year-to-date $3.8 billion, on track for high end of $4.8-$5.2 billion full-year, amid $162 billion funded backlog with 40% international.

Drivers: $2.1 billion operations cash from Missiles & Precision Weapons and Fixed-Wing, including $450 million NGAD/hypersonic milestones under Agile Combat Employment. Fixed-price dev contracts at 55% of backlog de-risk cash, EAC under 2%.

Working capital: DSO 65 days, inventory turns 4.2x via Supplier Collaboration Portal AI forecasting, saving $300 million YTD versus Boeing echoes.

CapEx $700 million or 3.2% sales: $250 million Fort Worth F-35 center for Lot 18-20; $150 million AM turbine blades (40% lead time cut); $100 million edge computing for DARPA SHiELD.

Utilization balances returns: $2.2 billion to shareholders YTD—$0.85/share dividend (1.8% yield, 50% payout); $1.5 billion buybacks retiring 2.1% shares at $285 average versus peers like Northrop at 18x EV/EBITDA.

Debt prepay $1.0 billion dropped net leverage to 1.8x EBITDA from 2.4x (A- S&P). Growth tuck-ins: $450 million UK counter-UAS for AUKUS drone defense; organic digital twins cut F-35 scrap 25%; insourcing rare earths.

U.S. strongest with $886 billion DoD, 65% backlog yielding $2.5 billion Q3 from hypersonics/space awareness like PrSM. Indo-Pacific +30% on $3.2 billion FMS to Japan/Australia for PAC-3 hedging Taiwan. Europe mixed: Ukraine +15% bookings, F-35 delays at 85% EBITDA conversion. Middle East: $1.1 billion THAAD for Saudi Vision 2030.

Forward, FCF margins to 12-14% FY26 via ERP 2.0 (10% WC cut), Huntsville/Palmdale AM centers (20% CapEx drop), sustainment playbook (75% margins). This underpins 10%+ EPS CAGR amid threats.

Maria Gonzalez:
Thank you, Steve. Operationally, we've seen significant supply chain improvements, increasing production rates on key programs like NGAD Lots and hypersonic glide vehicles. Our Supplier Collaboration Portal and nearshoring—70% of criticals including Polish titanium JV—have cut lead times 40%, enabling 98% glide-body yields and 15% touch labor reductions via cobots and AeroLean 2.0 across U.S. and India sites. We're investing in automation, digital twins, and apprenticeship programs with 2,500 hires for hypersonic fab and welder skills, driving inventory turns to 4.2x and $320 million savings. Specifically, Fort Worth F-35 expansion and Groton welding efficiencies position us for 2.0 subs/year by 2028, while digital engineering accelerates EAC by 25%.

Dr. Raj Patel:
To complement that, our tech infusion via the Enterprise Digital Backbone—$450 million invested—includes AI-optimized aerodynamics, software-defined avionics, and Siemens NX simulations cutting test costs 25%. Digital twins on 70% engine base reduce removals 25%, and additive nozzles/manufacturing derisk propulsion and blades, supporting NGAD open architecture for JADC2 and loyal wingmen.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one. Our first question comes from John Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on the program margins and cost performance analysis, especially any segment-specific risks heading into Q4?

David Reynolds:
Certainly, John. As Steve detailed, our 120 bps expansion to 11.8% reflects fixed-price maturity and cost-outs like 15% labor reductions on F-47 via automation. Defense at 12.4% benefits from CPI 1.05, though THAAD's titanium hit was isolated. Commercial's 200 bps gain from AeroLean cobots offsets OEM snarls. Q4 guide 12.0-12.3% assumes no major CR delays; our 92% fixed-price backlog and passthroughs cover inflation. Steve?

Steve Harlan:
Yes, John—to add, regional tailwinds like NDAA and NATO pledges support this, with tech like digital twins accelerating convergence 25%. Labor mitigated via apprenticeships.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Lee with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Sarah Lee:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about revenue and earnings guidance by segment—how does the aftermarket growth factor into commercial outlook?

Steve Harlan:
Sarah, great question. Commercial guidance $5.8-$6.0 billion incorporates 22% aftermarket surge to $1.6 billion, with Digital Twin LTSAs locking multi-year streams at 28%+ margins. Defense $11.2-$11.5 billion on 62% priority programs; Space steady at 10.5-11.0%. Aftermarket's 17% overall growth, now 42% mix, de-risks cyclicality—$50 billion backlog gives 3.5x coverage.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Chen with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Chen:
Thanks. Regarding the performance of priority defense programs, any updates on NGAD exports or hypersonic scaling?

Dr. Raj Patel:
Mike, excellent point. NGAD revenues up 22% to $1.1 billion, with 95% Block 4 acceptance and TR-3 tests progressing; UK/Japan GCAP exports build $4.2 billion backlog via open architecture for wingmen. Hypersonics $650 million, Lot 2 FRP on 98% yields, $250 million R&D for Mach 12+ against peers. AUKUS and FMS accelerate Indo-Pacific.

David Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation across hypersonics, NGAD, and services.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 earnings call. A replay and transcript will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
